articles.headline: Musk Says Ukraine Broke Starlink Rules; Ukraine Says Physics Already Did the Job
articles.dek: After a throttling that disrupted drone operations, SpaceX's owner alleged offensive use of the service, while Ukrainian officials say the commercial version cannot technically do what he describes.
articles.catch_up: Nearly two weeks ago, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of limiting the military's satellite internet service, disrupting drone missions and operations. Elon Musk has now said Ukraine violated Starlink's terms of service, and Ukraine denies it.
articles.why_it_matters: A single private company's settings can affect how a national military communicates in wartime, and the public currently has only competing statements to explain why. Governments relying on commercial infrastructure are learning that the terms of service are also a foreign policy document.
body: Elon Musk said this week that Ukraine's military broke Starlink's terms of service by using the network for offensive drone strikes, and that the loophole was closed last week, according to The Verge. Ukrainian officials say that did not happen and that it is not possible. It is a rare dispute in which one side cites a user agreement and the other cites speed limits.

The statement arrived nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of placing limits on the military's service that disrupted drone missions. Axios reported that Ukraine uses Starlink for communications, logistics, and defense against incoming drones. For offensive missions, officials say, Ukraine uses Starshield. Translation: Starshield is the version of Starlink controlled by the US military, which is a different product with a different landlord.

Musk pointed to a post from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that referred to using Starlink in mid-range strikes against enemy military targets. Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor to Zelenskyy, answered on Telegram that Starlink's systems connect only to devices moving between 70 and 90 kilometers per hour, about 43 to 55 miles per hour, and do not work in Russia. In his words, Ukraine therefore "physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes." A drone that is slower than a highway commute is apparently the only kind commercial Starlink was built to tolerate.

Ars Technica pointed to a further explanation from Serhii Sternenko, a former Ukrainian advisor. He said stationary terminals could be registered by military personnel or civilians, but any terminal working on the move had to be added to a special list and connected to Starshield. His conclusion was that civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. If true, the alleged violation would require a feature the product does not have.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield services had been fully restored. The Kyiv Independent reported that with the restriction lifted, the military can again connect to devices traveling faster than 400 km/h, about 248 mph. That is the difference between a throttle and no throttle, measured in drones.

The question of who pulled the lever remains untidy. Musk initially shifted blame for the slowdown to the US government, per The Verge. President Donald Trump responded that he was not involved and did not know who throttled SpaceX's services. The Wall Street Journal later reported that Trump asked Musk to lift the restrictions, which suggests that someone knew where the dial was.

So the current account is that a restriction was imposed, blamed on Washington, disowned by Washington, justified by a terms-of-service violation Kyiv says is technically impossible, and then lifted. Watch for whether anyone explains the dial in writing, or whether it stays an informal arrangement between a CEO and a war.
articles.wire_headline: Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service

articles.headline: Apple Updates iMac and MacBook Pro With M6 Chip, Skips M5 Entirely
articles.dek: The iMac jumps from the M4 straight to the M6, while the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro gets a single chip option and a larger storage ceiling.
articles.catch_up: Apple introduced its M6 chip in the Mac mini several weeks ago and is now spreading it across more of its computer lineup. The iMac and the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro are the latest to get it, according to Ars Technica.
articles.why_it_matters: Anyone with an older iMac or an entry-level MacBook Pro now has a clear reason to ask whether their machine is still current. The configuration limits also show how much Apple's naming and port choices decide what you can buy.
body: Apple announced refreshed versions of the iMac and the entry-level, 14-inch MacBook Pro, both now running the M6 chip, Ars Technica reported. The chip debuted in the Mac mini several weeks ago, so this is less a launch than a rollout. Apple has finished the first showing and is now moving the chip through the rest of the house.

The iMac gets the more dramatic change. Its previous update brought the M4, and Apple skipped the M5 and went straight to the M6. Translation: if you own an M4 iMac, you are now two generations behind, despite the fact that no M5 iMac ever existed for you to be behind.

The iMac comes in two chip variants, and the distinction is oddly specific. Choose the "M6 chip with two Thunderbolt ports" and you get a 10-core CPU and a 10-core GPU, with a ceiling of 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. Choose the "M6 chip with four Thunderbolt ports" and you get 12 cores of each, plus up to 32GB of RAM and 2TB of storage.

Translation: the number of ports on the back of your computer now determines how much memory it is allowed to have. Ars Technica did not say why the options are bundled this way. Shoppers who want more memory must also accept more ports, and shoppers who want more ports must also accept more processor cores.

The MacBook Pro is simpler. There is one M6 option, with a 12-core CPU and a 12-core GPU, capped at 32GB of RAM but available with up to 4TB of storage. That is a menu with one chip on it, which is at least easy to read.

As for performance, Ars Technica noted that Apple's claims for the Mac mini applied here: up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, up to double the graphics performance, and nearly five times faster on-device AI, compared with the M4. Those figures largely matched what Ars saw when it tested the M6 Mac mini last month, and it expects new iMac users to see similar numbers. Note that these are comparisons against the M4, so MacBook Pro owners should check which chip they have before doing the math.
The practical advice is the usual one. If your machine works, the M6 will still be there next year, and Apple will still be skipping something.
articles.wire_headline: Apple refreshes the iMac, entry-level MacBook Pro with the M6 chip

articles.headline: Treasury Yields Top 5% as Washington Plans to Fix Deficit Sometime After Everyone Retires
articles.dek: A $1.992 trillion deficit and a 10-year yield above 5% are squeezing mortgages, while economists expect the Fed to do nothing this week and something later.
articles.catch_up: The U.S. ran a deficit of $1.992 trillion in fiscal 2026, and the 10-year Treasury yield has climbed about 114 basis points since the Iran war began on Feb. 28. The Fed meets this week, and CNBC's survey says it will hold rates steady.
articles.why_it_matters: The 10-year yield sets the tone for mortgage rates, now around 7.5%, so government borrowing costs show up in the price of a house. The sources also suggest the political gridlock after the midterms makes a fiscal fix unlikely for years.
body: The U.S. government borrowed $1.992 trillion more than it collected in fiscal 2026, up 12% from last year, according to Treasury data cited by CNBC. That equals roughly 6.2% of gross domestic product. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued for a deficit below 4% of GDP by the end of President Trump's term, which is a target CNBC says there is almost no way of hitting.

Meanwhile, the 10-year Treasury yield sat at 5.1% on Friday by CNBC's account, and 5.0% in the latest official data. Translation: the 10-year yield is the interest rate the government pays to borrow for a decade, and the rest of the economy borrows at a markup to it. It has risen 114 basis points, or 1.14 percentage points, since the end of February.

The causes are plentiful. The Iran war pushed up oil and diesel prices, which leads bond traders to demand more yield in case central banks raise rates. Investors also want extra pay for holding long-term bonds because they expect more of them to keep arriving. Companies are issuing hundreds of billions in debt to build AI infrastructure, so the Treasury is competing for the same pool of money as every data center with a bond underwriter.

The ordinary-person version: the average 30-year mortgage is about 7.5%, and Redfin said pending home sales fell 4% in September, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Translation: the government's borrowing habit has become your down payment's problem.

The math gets worse from here. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that rates a half-point above its forecast would add $1.9 trillion to deficits over ten years, and 1.5 points above would add $6 trillion. The CBO expects the 10-year to average 4.3% over that period, versus 5.1% today.

Bessent's proposed solution is growth. "We have to grow our way out of it," he said in Dallas last month, pointing to artificial intelligence. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget calculates that growth alone would need a decade of 7.2% annual expansion. Second-quarter GDP was recently revised up to 2.2% annualized, so the gap is a mere five percentage points a year, sustained for ten years.

The Fed offers no relief this week. In CNBC's survey of 30 fund managers, strategists and economists, 93% expect a pause, and 76% expect a hike in December. Respondents are split on whether that is wise. Richard Bernstein of Janus Henderson called the Fed's hesitancy to raise rates "unfathomable." Mark Zandi of Moody's Analytics said this isn't the time for more hikes, citing falling real wages and a shaky AI-fueled stock market.

Politics does not offer much either. Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House, and the survey puts Democratic control of both chambers as the most likely outcome. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely next speaker, wants to reverse $1 trillion in healthcare cuts, while Trump pledged $5,000 checks to adults if Republicans swept the election. These positions are not close, in the way Earth and Neptune are not close.

CNBC notes that expensive borrowing is not the same as a crisis, and higher yields are also drawing buyers to Treasuries. Total debt reached $40 trillion this year, and nobody knows precisely what level is unsustainable. The country is therefore running an experiment to find out, with the results due at an unspecified time.
articles.wire_headline: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge

articles.headline: Boeing Beats Quarter, Misses Future, and Investors Choose to Sell the Future
articles.dek: Boeing's stock fell 10% after it pushed its $10 billion free cash flow target to 2029 and said 737 Max output will not hit 52 a month until late 2027.
articles.catch_up: Boeing has spent years trying to recover from production and quality problems, and CEO Kelly Ortberg has been steadying the 737 Max line. On Tuesday the company reported third-quarter results and, for the first time, gave investors free cash flow targets for the next three years.
articles.why_it_matters: Boeing's cash flow depends on delivering planes, and delivery pace affects airline fleet plans, aircraft availability and the stock held in many retirement portfolios. A slower ramp means a slower recovery, and the company is telling investors so directly.
body: Boeing shares fell 10% on Tuesday after the company reported third-quarter results and then described what the next three years of cash will look like. According to CNBC, the stock hit a fresh 52-week low and was on pace for its worst day since the April 2025 tariff panic. The quarter itself was fine. The forecast was the problem, which is a common arrangement in markets, where the past is a receipt and the future is the invoice.

The quarter, briefly: revenue rose 4% to $24.19 billion, ahead of the $23.84 billion analysts expected, per LSEG. The adjusted loss was 34 cents a share, worse than the expected 21 cents. Free cash flow was $464 million, up from $238 million a year earlier and above the $330 million FactSet consensus. Translation: free cash flow is the cash left after a company pays to run and build things, and with Boeing not yet reliably profitable, it is the number investors watch most.

Then came the outlook. Boeing expects $3 billion of free cash flow in 2027 against a consensus of $5.7 billion, and $6 billion in 2028 against $9.6 billion. It still reaches its $10 billion annual target in 2029, but CNBC's analysis notes that is a year later than Wall Street had modeled, and the 2029 consensus was $12.9 billion. Part of the 2027 shortfall comes from extra spending to support the Navy's next-generation F/A-XX fighter contract, which Boeing won in September. Winning a large contract means paying up front for the privilege.

The main constraint is wings. Ortberg said Boeing is producing about 47 737 Max jets a month and now aims for 52 in the second half of 2027. He said wing output is improving but must show sustained performance first. Boeing also now expects to fall short of its goal of delivering 500 737s in 2026. This matters because, as CNBC noted, most of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it. A plane that is nearly finished is, financially, a very large decoration.

The commercial airplane unit shows the strain. Revenue fell 3% to $10.72 billion, with an operating margin of negative 6.5%, which Boeing attributed to delivery mix, costs tied to future production rate changes and higher supply chain costs. Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes, one more than a year earlier. The defense unit did the heavy lifting, with revenue up 15% to $7.94 billion.

There was good news, delivered at a lower volume. Boeing reported a record $745 billion backlog, and the FAA certified the 737 Max 10 last week after the Max 7 in August, completing the family. Ortberg said customer demand has not changed despite the Middle East conflict pushing up jet fuel prices, and argued that costly fuel makes efficient new jets more attractive. Brent crude was most recently listed at $115.22, so airlines have a strong incentive to retire thirsty old planes, if they can get new ones.

CNBC's analysts called the report a clearing event and kept their buy-equivalent rating, but cut their price target to $225. Their logic is that bad news is now priced in and Ortberg is deliberately under-promising. That is a reasonable view, and also the view of every investor who has ever bought a falling stock.

Ortberg told CNBC that everyone wants Boeing to go faster but that it will do it right. After the company's recent history, that is the correct answer. It also happens to be the answer that costs $2.7 billion less in 2027 than investors hoped.
articles.wire_headline: The big reason Boeing’s stock is falling so hard after earnings

articles.headline: SK Hynix Earns 83 Trillion Won in a Quarter, Then Gives Much of It Back
articles.dek: The South Korean memory maker posted record third-quarter profit and promised about 100 trillion won to shareholders, as AI demand keeps outrunning the supply of chips.
articles.catch_up: SK Hynix makes memory chips, including the high-bandwidth memory that sits next to AI processors in data centers. On Wednesday it reported third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations and announced a large shareholder payout.
articles.why_it_matters: Memory is a bottleneck for the AI buildout, so SK Hynix's results suggest demand is still strong and that prices for chips in servers and devices may stay high. For investors, a payout this size is a signal about how much cash the company thinks the boom will keep producing.
body: SK Hynix reported record quarterly results on Wednesday, with revenue of 104.62 trillion won ($78.86 billion) against the 98.34 trillion won that LSEG SmartEstimates had expected, CNBC reported. Operating profit came in at 83.33 trillion won versus 76.72 trillion expected. Shares rose more than 8%, ahead of the Kospi's 6.25% gain, which is what happens when a company is both the news and the index.

Translation: LSEG SmartEstimates weight the forecasts of analysts who have been right more often, so the company beat the estimates of the people who are good at estimating. Revenue rose 327.9% from a year earlier and operating profit climbed 632.1%. Sales passed 100 trillion won for the first time, a milestone that required a number with a lot of zeros to be called small by the time of the next report.

The company then decided what to do with the money. It plans to return about 100 trillion won to shareholders, including at least 30 trillion won in cash dividends and 60 trillion won in buybacks and cancellations. Translation: a buyback is when a company purchases its own shares, and cancelling them means the remaining shares each own a slightly bigger slice of the business. It is a way of saying that the best investment available is itself.

The third-quarter dividend is 14 trillion won, including a special dividend funded by gains from SK Hynix's investment in Japanese chipmaker Kioxia. CEO Kwak Noh-Jung said the company intends to return those gains to shareholders. A further 20 trillion won buyback is planned, half of it to be cancelled this year, after a previously announced 40 trillion won buyback finished last week. The company also raised its shareholder return target to more than 50% of cumulative free cash flow from 2025 to 2027.

One thing it will not be doing is taking its U.S. subsidiary Solidigm public. Kwak cited financial market volatility and a correction in semiconductor stocks, and said an IPO would not fully deliver the anticipated benefits at this time. Translation: the market was in a mood, and the company had enough cash that it did not need to ask strangers for more.

The operating details explain the cash. HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, is the specialized memory used alongside AI processors to move large amounts of data. SK Hynix expects its sixth-generation HBM4, which began mass production and shipments in the third quarter, to surpass HBM3E in both shipments and revenue in the fourth quarter. Average selling prices for DRAM rose by a high-20s percentage from the previous quarter, and shipments of server DDR5 chips rose more than 40%.

For customers, the outlook is less comfortable. The company said demand outpaces supply in the memory market and expects that imbalance to continue for the time being. It has long-term agreements with 14 major customers covering more than 50% of its 2027 and 2028 capacity, and expects demand to outpace supply through 2030. Translation: buyers are reserving chips years before they exist, which is the semiconductor version of booking a restaurant table two years out.

The company also plans to significantly increase investment next year, which sits a little awkwardly beside a 100 trillion won payout. Shareholders get cash now, the factories get expanded later, and the open question is what happens to both promises if the AI spending that funds them slows. For now, SK Hynix says the shortage is the plan.
articles.wire_headline: SK Hynix shares soar over 8% as profit beats, chipmaker to return $25 billion to investors

articles.headline: Corporate America Finds Consumer 'Resilient,' Mostly Because the Word Is Free
articles.dek: Third-quarter earnings from Coca-Cola, UPS and Royal Caribbean point to steady spending, while Whirlpool and Sherwin-Williams report something closer to endurance.
articles.catch_up: Third-quarter earnings season has started, and companies are describing the U.S. consumer as holding up despite record diesel prices, high borrowing costs and tension with Iran. CNBC reported that retail sales rose 0.8% in September after a 1.3% jump in August.
articles.why_it_matters: Consumer spending drives most of the U.S. economy, so whether households keep buying shapes jobs, inflation and the odds of a slowdown. The early reports suggest spending is intact, but some of it reflects higher prices rather than more stuff.
body: Several large U.S. companies reported third-quarter results this week, and according to CNBC, one word kept turning up: resilient. Royal Caribbean, UPS, Coca-Cola, Sherwin-Williams and even Whirlpool used it or something close to it. It is an efficient word, since it can describe a booming business and a shrinking one with equal confidence.

Start with the cheerful cases. Royal Caribbean carried 2.7 million guests in the quarter, up 9% from a year earlier, and said bookings for 2027 were already "up in the high teens." CEO Jason Liberty told CNBC that even through challenges, the consumer "comes roaring back." Translation: people who booked a cruise would like to keep their cruise. Shares closed up more than 5% on Tuesday.

UPS beat expectations on earnings and revenue, with U.S. revenue up 4.5% to $14.86 billion. It raised its full-year revenue forecast for the second quarter in a row, to about $92.6 billion from $91.2 billion. CEO Carol Tomé called consumers resilient heading into the holidays, though the company also expects fourth-quarter domestic daily volume to fall because it is shrinking its Amazon deliveries. That is a decline the company chose, which is the most flattering kind.

Coca-Cola beat estimates and raised its outlook, now expecting comparable earnings per share to grow at least 11%, up from 9% to 10%. North American unit case volume was flat. Translation: Americans bought the same number of cases, at higher prices, which the company classifies as steady demand. CFO John Murphy told CNBC that shoppers at every income level are "looking for value," a phrase that means they are comparing prices and still choosing soda.

Then there is the less resilient end of the resilience spectrum. Sherwin-Williams beat on revenue but missed on earnings per share. Sales rose 7.9%, which the company attributed to higher selling prices, while raw materials and supply-chain costs ate into profit. It kept its full-year guidance and said customer sentiment points to "muted demand" through 2027. In plain terms, the paint is more expensive and the walls are not getting painted faster.

Whirlpool missed on both revenue and profit, cut its full-year revenue guidance, and reported North American net sales down more than 8%. Its CFO nonetheless cited the "balance sheet resilience" of the company. Shares still closed up more than 3%, suggesting investors had expected something worse and rewarded the company for delivering it.

The backdrop explains the nervousness. CNBC reported diesel hit a record $6.52 per gallon in September, and economists feared that costly gas, high borrowing costs and U.S.-Iran tension would make shoppers pull back. Official data show Brent crude at $115.22, the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.0% and CPI inflation at 3.74% year over year. September's retail sales were also boosted by spending at gas stations, meaning part of the strength is people paying more to drive to the stores.

The pattern is a consumer who is still spending, but increasingly on cruises and cola rather than washing machines and paint. Watch the holiday-season guidance next. If "resilient" is still the word in January, it will either be true or very well rehearsed.
articles.wire_headline: Early third-quarter earnings show a 'resilient' U.S. consumer, with signs of strain

articles.headline: Administration Eases Russian Diesel Sanctions to Lower Pump Prices Before Tuesday's Midterms
articles.dek: A deal with Moscow will add roughly 75,000 to 124,000 barrels a day to a market that burns 28 million, which analysts say will not materially lower prices.
articles.catch_up: Fuel prices have spiked since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, and the administration now faces voters in next Tuesday's midterm elections. President Trump struck a deal with Vladimir Putin letting Russia export diesel under a U.S. sanctions waiver.
articles.why_it_matters: Drivers and businesses that depend on diesel should not expect relief at the pump from this deal, according to analysts cited by CNBC. The episode also shows how election-year price pressure can shape sanctions policy toward a country the U.S. is trying to pressure over Ukraine.
body: The Trump administration has suspended U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Tuesday that more Russian fuel could be allowed onto the market depending on Moscow's behavior. He described the suspension as "an incentive" for Russia to end the war in Ukraine. Fuel is, in this arrangement, both the reward and the thing voters are angry about.

According to CNBC, the deal calls for Russia to export 800,000 metric tons of diesel in October and November, followed by another million tons. Translation: a metric ton is a unit of weight, and diesel is normally traded by volume, so analysts converted. The first shipment of 300,000 tons works out to about 75,000 barrels per day if spread over a month. The second, 500,000 tons, equals about 124,000 barrels per day.

Global demand is around 28 million barrels per day, so the headline volumes amount to a rounding error with a flag on it. Analysts told CNBC the deal will not materially lower prices. Wright himself said it would help with supplies only "on the margin," which is the economist's way of saying a little, eventually, maybe.

The logistics are already underway. MarineTraffic shows the Russian-flagged tanker Talisman expected on the U.S. East Coast on Nov. 9, five days after the election. Another tanker, the Leruo, has left Russia bound for the "Atlantic Coast" without saying whether that means America. Wright said more tankers could "quite possibly" follow, and described the policy as "trying to put a carrot in front of Russia."

The carrot is awkward for several reasons. Ukraine has been striking Russian refineries this year to reduce the revenue the Kremlin earns from energy exports, and those strikes forced Moscow to impose a diesel export ban in July. The Kremlin has partially lifted that ban to honor the deal with Trump. Ukraine's campaign to reduce Russian diesel sales and Washington's campaign to buy some of it are therefore running at the same time.

President Zelenskyy has sharply criticized the arrangement. Several Republican senators joined Democratic colleagues in a letter calling it "a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies." It is rare for the Senate to agree on anything, and the subject it found is a diesel waiver.

Meanwhile, MarketWatch reports that Trump has continued to tout the fortunes U.S. energy companies have made during the Iran war while campaigning for Republican candidates. The same report says consumers face the most expensive year for gas prices ever. Brent crude was last recorded at $115.22, and CPI inflation stood at 3.74% year over year in September. Producers are celebrating the price level and motorists are paying it, which is the standard division of labor.
The kicker arrives next week. The election is Tuesday, the first tanker docks Nov. 9, and the oil market will go on needing 28 million barrels a day regardless of who wins.
articles.wire_headline: As Trump touts energy companies’ fortunes, U.S. consumers face the most expensive year for gas prices ever
